topic.title: The ₹350 chair
topic.claim: Half of what you pay for café coffee is rent on a chair, because our cities have almost nowhere free to sit.
topic.moment: You buy a cold coffee you don't want so you can take a call for an hour.

turn.actually: We're paying for a seat, a plug and Wi-Fi, with the coffee as the ticket.

topic.feeling: Like I'm paying an entry fee to exist in my own city.
topic.villain: Cities with almost no free public places to sit: few libraries, parks or plazas
topic.because: When the only places to sit are ones that sell something, the café can price the seat. The menu is just how it bills you.
topic.payoff: Would you buy that coffee if you could sit in a park with Wi-Fi? Then you know what you paid for.
topic.behaviour: People work, date and take calls from cafés, buying one drink per hour as rent.
topic.mechanism: Scarce free space lets private places charge for sitting.
topic.group: Young professionals in metros, often in shared flats
topic.send_to: The friend who 'works from a café' three days a week
topic.why_now: Hybrid work has filled cafés with laptops on weekdays.
real_details: A r/hyderabad post says the poster doesn't want more cafes and wants clean parks and public spaces instead. The thread text includes no comments, numbers or personal stories.

score.why: The café coffee is the ticket for a chair. Cities with nowhere free to sit explain it, and the line reads as an everyday observation, not a complaint.

violations: 12. Slide 9: "That's what the coffee is worth. Everything else was rent." This is stated as fact and is wrong. The sources put a café's real rent at roughly 15-20% of revenue (Blue Tokai about 17%). The rest of the price covers beans, staff and margin. The post never says "half", but "everything else" is stronger than the topic's own claim, which the sources already contradict.

16. Slide 6: "Here's what's going on underneath." This is stock scaffolding where fresh words should carry the turn. Slide 7's "Anyone who has worked on pricing knows this" is also a vague insider-credential line standing in for the actual mechanism.
notes: slide 9: Don't say "everything else was rent". Reframe it as a seat premium: whatever you'd pay beyond the coffee's worth is the price of the chair. Keep the park-with-shade-and-Wi-Fi test, but end on a line people can repeat, not an accounting claim the sources contradict.

slides 5-7: The same idea (the seat gets a price) is said three times, and slide 7 is a generic pricing line. Merge them into one slide. Drop "Here's what's going on underneath" and "Anyone who has worked on pricing knows this". Name the mechanism plainly: when every place to sit also sells something, the café can charge for the sitting, and the menu is how it bills you.

slide 6 or 7: Add one sourced fact that makes the point bigger and is true. A café's real rent is only about 15-20% of its revenue (2019 industry reporting; Blue Tokai FY25 is about 17%). So the landlord isn't what you're paying for. You're paying for how few alternatives you have. This adds the new insight the post lacks and fixes the accuracy problem.

slides 5 and 8: The prices don't match. Slide 5 gives three hours for about ₹700, which is roughly ₹230 an hour. Slide 8 says "₹280 an hour", but ₹280 is the price of one drink. Use one consistent figure. For example: "You paid ₹280 for the drink and the hour came free."

slides 3-4: Slide 3 has three examples but is generic (laptop crowd, couple, flatmate). Slide 4 has the one real insider detail, the staff wiping your table. Give slide 4 more weight, add one more detail only a regular would notice (the plug seat that opens up, the Wi-Fi password printed on the bill), and cut slide 2's closing "You barely drank half", which repeats what the ice already shows.

violations: Slide 7: "And most of it isn't the landlord's cut... You're paying for having nowhere else to go." The post shows rent is only 15-20% (Blue Tokai 17%), then says the rest of the bill is the price of the chair. Nothing shows that. Staff, beans, margin and other costs fill the gap. The seat-pricing mechanism is asserted rather than shown, and the cited figure weakens the thesis instead of backing it (hard failure 12, with a thin 'because').
notes: slide 7: The rent figure does not prove the chair is what you pay for. Either drop the percentages and the 'most of it' jump, or use them honestly: rent is a small slice, so the café isn't charging you rent on the seat. Then make the real because explicit. Free places to sit are so rare that a café can sell the sitting itself, and the café bills it as a drink. The topic's 'because' already says this. Don't claim a share of the bill that the sources can't back.

slide 9 and 10: The park test carries the turn. Sharpen it so it lands as the because. The café can price the seat only because the park next door has no shade, no plug and no Wi-Fi. That makes the villain the city, not the café, and the post is stronger for it. Keep the last line as a test, but cut one 'chair' repetition so it stings instead of explaining.

sources.fact: Blue Tokai's FY25 rent expense was Rs 55.16 crore on revenue of Rs 332.7 crore, about 17% of revenue. That is well below half, which contradicts the claim. The percentage is my own calculation from the two figures.
sources.excerpt: reported a 50% year-on-year increase in revenue to Rs 332.7 crore in FY25, up from Rs 221 crore in FY24. ... the rent expense of the company surged 67%, to Rs 55.16 crore in FY25, up from Rs 33 crore in FY24.

sources.fact: Industry reporting puts rent at roughly 15-20% of a coffee shop's revenue, and up to 25% in prime locations, not 50%. The article is from 2019.
sources.excerpt: Rentals, as a percentage of operating costs, have more than doubled in the last few years and eat away almost 15-20 per cent ... In prime locales, it even goes as high as 25 per cent.
